title: You can delete the platform in seconds. You can silence the notifications. You can disappear from the feed. But what happens when the screen goes dark…and the hunger to be noticed is still alive?
paragraphs: You can delete the platform in seconds. You can silence the notifications. You can disappear from the feed. But what happens when the screen goes dark…and the hunger to be noticed is still alive?
You deleted the app.
Maybe you finally got tired of it.
Tired of checking.
Tired of scrolling.
Tired of watching people you barely know live lives that somehow made your own feel smaller.
Tired of posting something and pretending you did not care whether anyone reacted to it…while quietly checking five minutes later.
Then ten.
Then twenty.
Maybe you hated what social media was doing to you.
So you deleted it.
And for a moment, it felt like freedom.
No notifications.
No follower counts.

No endless parade of vacations, engagements, promotions, perfect marriages, transformed bodies, expensive dinners, successful ministries, smiling children, beautiful houses, and carefully edited lives.
Silence.
Finally.
But then something uncomfortable happened.
The app disappeared…
and the ache didn't.
You still noticed who complimented you.
You still replayed conversations wondering what people thought about you.
You still felt strangely wounded when somebody else received the attention you secretly wanted.
You still wanted to be impressive.
Still wanted to be admired.
Still wanted somebody to notice how hard you were trying.
Still wanted to walk into a room and matter.
And perhaps that is when the real question begins.
What if the app was never the deepest problem?
What if it was merely a mirror?
What if deleting Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, or whatever platform consumed you removed one outlet for the hunger…but never confronted the hunger itself?
Because an appetite for human approval does not need Wi-Fi to survive.
It can migrate.
From followers to coworkers.
From likes to compliments.
From comments to applause.
From strangers online to people at church.
From posting photographs to displaying spirituality.
From wanting people to admire your appearance to wanting Christians to admire your holiness.
You can leave social media and still perform.
You can put the phone down and still compare.
You can stop posting selfies and start posting righteousness.
You can stop chasing followers and begin chasing the approval of religious people.
And suddenly an ancient sentence written by the apostle Paul becomes painfully modern.
“For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.”
Galatians 1:10, KJV.
The Greek presses even closer.
“Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν Θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην.”
There is a word in that sentence worth sitting with: “ἀρέσκειν” — areskein — from areskō, carrying the sense of pleasing, satisfying, or seeking to please.
Paul is not saying that kindness is sinful.
He is not commanding Christians to become abrasive, insensitive, or deliberately offensive.

Scripture itself tells believers, “Let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification” (Romans 15:2, KJV). Paul elsewhere says that he seeks the good of others so that they may be saved (1 Corinthians 10:33).
So Galatians 1:10 cannot honestly mean, “I should never care how my actions affect another person.”
The issue is deeper.
Who sits on the throne of your obedience?
Whose approval becomes decisive when pleasing people and obeying Christ collide?
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because some of us do not merely enjoy approval.
We feed on it.
A compliment can carry us for hours.
Criticism can ruin an entire day.
Being overlooked can feel like rejection.
Watching somebody else succeed can awaken something ugly that we immediately try to rename.
“I’m just discouraged.”
Maybe.
But sometimes discouragement is wounded pride wearing respectable clothes.
Sometimes we are not devastated because God was dishonored.
We are devastated because somebody else was noticed.
Sometimes we call it loneliness when what we desperately want is an audience.
Sometimes we call it “sharing our journey” when underneath the sharing is a trembling question:
Do you see me?
Do I matter?
Am I attractive enough?
Successful enough?
Spiritual enough?
Interesting enough?
Loved enough?
Please…
somebody tell me I am enough.
And that is where the Gospel walks into the room.
Not carrying another self-esteem slogan.
Not telling you to stare into a mirror and convince yourself that everybody else is wrong.
The Gospel gives you something infinitely stronger than the applause of strangers.
It gives you Christ.
There is a reason human approval makes such a cruel master.
It changes constantly.
Yesterday they celebrated you.
Today they forgot you.
Yesterday the post performed well.
Today nobody seems interested.
Yesterday somebody called you inspiring.
Tomorrow the same person may misunderstand you.
Build your identity on applause and you will eventually become terrified of silence.
Build it on admiration and criticism will feel like death.
Build it on being seen and being overlooked will feel unbearable.
But Jesus offers an identity that does not rise and fall with an algorithm.
Consider the scandal of the Gospel.
The Son of God was rejected.
“He is despised and rejected of men” (Isaiah 53:3, KJV).
The One whose approval actually matters entered a world obsessed with status and willingly walked toward humiliation.
Jesus was mocked.
Spat upon.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Crucified.
Crowds that could gather around Him could also turn against Him.
Yet Christ did not need public approval to tell Him who He was.
At His baptism, before the public ministry that would make His name known throughout the region, the Father declared:
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
Matthew 3:17, KJV.
Before the miracles multiplied.
Before the crowds swelled.
Before Calvary.
Beloved.
There is something here our approval-starved generation desperately needs to understand.
Jesus did not go to the cross so you could become impressive.
He went to the cross to save sinners.
You do not need a better personal brand nearly as much as you need reconciliation with God.
And reconciliation does not come through followers.
It comes through Christ.
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
1 Timothy 2:5, KJV.
Your deepest problem is not low engagement.
It is sin.
And your greatest hope is not greater visibility.
It is grace.
That changes everything.
Because now you can finally admit the embarrassing things.
You can admit that sometimes you wanted the photograph to make somebody jealous.
You can admit that you checked who viewed the story.
You can admit that somebody else's success bothered you.
You can admit that you exaggerated because the ordinary truth did not seem impressive enough.
You can admit that you have occasionally performed happiness while privately falling apart.
You can even admit something more frightening.
Sometimes you wanted people to think you were close to God more than you actually wanted to be close to God.
That one hurts.
Because religious approval can become just as intoxicating as worldly approval.
Jesus warned about people who did righteous acts “to be seen of men” (Matthew 6:1).
Think about those words.
“To be seen.”
Two thousand years before social media, Jesus was already exposing the heart behind spiritual performance.
He spoke about charitable giving that could become theater.
Prayer that could become theater.
Fasting that could become theater.
The technology changed.
The human heart did not.
You can turn even Christianity into content designed primarily to make people admire you.
You can know when to say “Amen.”
Know which verse to post.
Know how to sound broken without actually repenting.
Know how to look surrendered while secretly being addicted to recognition.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave that hidden.
Grace does not merely comfort.
Grace exposes before it heals.
Not to humiliate you for entertainment.
To free you.
Because imagine the freedom of no longer needing every room to notice you.
Imagine being able to celebrate someone else's blessing without secretly wondering why God passed over you.
Imagine obeying Jesus when nobody applauds.
Giving when nobody knows.
Praying when nobody hears.
Serving when nobody posts a photograph.
Forgiving when nobody congratulates you.
Remaining faithful when obedience makes you less popular rather than more popular.
That is freedom.
Not becoming indifferent to people.
Becoming liberated from needing people to function as your god.
Proverbs 29:25 says, “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.”
A snare.
That is such an accurate word.
Approval promises belonging and quietly builds a cage.
Soon you edit yourself before speaking.
You hide convictions because somebody might unfollow you.
You soften truths Christ has made clear because obedience could cost social acceptance.
Or you swing in the opposite direction and become needlessly provocative because outrage gives you another kind of attention.
Either way, people are still controlling you.
That is why the answer is not merely deleting an app.
Sometimes deleting the app may be wise.
Jesus taught radical seriousness about removing occasions of sin (Matthew 5:29–30). Scripture repeatedly calls believers to wisdom, self-control, and vigilance.
Set the boundary.
Turn off the notifications.
Unfollow what repeatedly drags your heart toward envy.
Take the break.
Put the phone outside the bedroom.
Do whatever wise boundary helps you walk faithfully.
But do not confuse pruning the branch with healing the root.
You can delete the app tonight and reinstall approval addiction tomorrow under another name.
The deeper prayer sounds more like this:
Jesus, why do I need them to notice me?
Why does their silence hurt this much?
Why am I threatened when somebody else shines?
Why do I keep rehearsing what people might think about me?
Why am I more frightened of disappointing them than disobeying You?
Why do I want to be seen?
And then comes the question many of us would rather avoid.
What am I trying to get from strangers that I should be receiving from God?
Maybe you have been carrying rejection for years.
Maybe somebody important made you feel invisible.
Maybe affection in your childhood had to be earned.
Maybe praise became proof that you were safe.
Maybe popularity became medicine for an old wound.
Those experiences can help explain why approval feels powerful.
But they cannot become your savior.
Jesus can meet you deeper than applause ever will.
He knows the version of you nobody follows.
The version without the lighting.
Without the filters.
Without the clever captions.
Without the Sunday smile.
Without the accomplishments.
Without the performance.
He sees the envy.
The vanity.
The insecurity.
The secret competition.
The desperation.
The shame.
And the astonishing message of Christianity is not that Jesus discovered the real you and walked away.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8, KJV.
While we were yet sinners.
Not once we became impressive.
Not once our image was repaired.
Not once everybody approved.
Christ died for sinners.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of healing.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who receives repentant sinners by grace.
You do not have to protect your image before Jesus.
There is nothing behind your carefully managed curtain that surprises Him.
Bring it into the light.
“God, I wanted their praise.”
Bring it.
“God, I was jealous.”
Bring it.
“God, I wanted to be admired.”
Bring it.
“God, I have been pretending.”
Bring it.
“God, I cared more about their opinion than Your Word.”
Bring it.
“God, forgive me.”
Bring that too.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9, KJV.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Because grace is greater.
Jesus does not merely rewrite your public reputation.
He begins transforming the heart underneath it.
And perhaps someday you will open social media again.
Perhaps you will not.
That is not ultimately the measure of victory.
The greater question is whether the platform remains on the throne after the app is gone.
Can you post without needing worship?
Can you disappear without feeling worthless?
Can you be corrected without collapsing?
Can somebody else receive applause while you sincerely rejoice?
Can you tell the truth even when truth costs approval?
Can you obey Jesus when the room becomes quiet?
Can you serve when nobody knows your name?
Because heaven is not measuring your worth in likes.
The cross has already exposed how worthless our self-made righteousness is—and how immeasurably costly the grace of God is.
So perhaps the next time your hand reaches instinctively toward your phone, stop for a moment.
Not because phones are inherently evil.
Because sometimes our reflexes reveal our hungers.
Ask yourself:
What am I looking for right now?
Connection?
Distraction?
Escape?
Comparison?
Validation?
Someone to tell me that I matter?
Then remember whose eyes matter eternally.
You are standing before God.
And if you are in Christ, your hope is not that you successfully convinced the world you were worthy.
Your hope is Jesus Christ—crucified for sinners, risen from the dead, reigning as Lord, and sufficient for everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
Maybe this article made you uncomfortable.
Good questions often do.
Sit with Galatians 1:10.
Ask the Holy Spirit to expose where human approval has quietly begun competing with obedience to Christ.
And if something hidden was exposed, be honest.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting this battle.
Save it too.

Approval addiction rarely dies after one moment of conviction. Come back when comparison returns. Come back when criticism stings. Come back when somebody else's success awakens jealousy. Come back when you are tempted to measure your value by attention again.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, and Jesus Christ, follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Let your sharing become mission rather than performance.
Come to Christ.
Because eventually every notification becomes silent.
Every trend disappears.
Every follower count stops increasing.
Every photograph ages.
Every platform changes.
Every human audience eventually looks somewhere else.
But the question of Galatians 1:10 remains.
Whose approval rules your heart?
You deleted the app.
Now bring Jesus the hunger that made you need the applause.
Because perhaps the freedom you were searching for was never hiding behind the delete button.
Perhaps it begins when you finally stop asking strangers to give you what only Christ can ultimately secure.
You were never created to spend your life auditioning for people who cannot save you.
